html:
Sukarno was the leader of Indonesia's struggle for independence from the Dutch and the country's first president, from 1945 to 1967. Like many Javanese he used one name only.

Born in Surabaya and trained as an engineer in Bandung, he became the most powerful speaker of the nationalist movement in the Dutch East Indies in the 1920s. He founded the Indonesian National Party in 1927, and the Dutch kept him in jail or exile for most of the next fifteen years.

The Japanese invasion of 1942 freed him. He worked with the occupiers, helping raise labour and troops for them, in return for a chance to spread nationalist ideas. Two days after Japan surrendered, he and Mohammad Hatta declared Indonesia independent on 17 August 1945. He led the four-year struggle against the returning Dutch, through war and diplomacy, until they recognised independence in 1949.

As president:

  • He gave the new state its ideology, Pancasila, five principles meant to unite a nation of many islands, languages and faiths.
  • He hosted the Bandung Conference of Asian and African states in 1955 with Nehru and others, a step toward the Non-Aligned Movement.
  • In 1959 he replaced parliamentary rule with "Guided Democracy", balancing the army against a large Communist Party.
  • He led a campaign of confrontation against the new state of Malaysia, while inflation ran out of control at home.

After a failed coup attempt in 1965, the army under Suharto took control, and hundreds of thousands of suspected communists were killed in 1965 and 1966. Sukarno was pushed aside and died under house arrest in 1970. He remains Indonesia's founding father.
